title: Verbs
intro: Match each verb to its subject and the time of the action.

sections.heading: Find the subject before you check agreement
body: Find the subject before choosing the verb. An intervening of, with, or along with phrase does not change the subject’s number.
Cross out the interruption: “The box of old letters is on the shelf.” Box controls is, not letters.

examples.text: The list of ingredients was longer than expected.
examples.label: Subject 'list' is singular, so 'was' is correct

examples.text: The list of ingredients were longer than expected.
examples.label: Verb wrongly agrees with 'ingredients,' the object of the preposition

sections.tip: Locate the head of the full subject, including when the subject follows the verb. Set aside intervening modifiers, then check number and tense against that actual subject.

sections.heading: Collective nouns and indefinite pronouns
body: Each, everyone, everybody, either, neither, and one take singular agreement, even with a plural phrase afterward: “Each of the players is ready.”
A collective noun acting as a single unit also takes singular agreement: “The committee votes tomorrow.” Check how the group functions in context.
With either X or Y and neither X nor Y, the nearer subject controls agreement: either the guides or the curator is speaking; either the curator or the guides are speaking.

examples.text: Everyone on the committees has signed the form.
examples.label: 'Everyone' is singular; the plural 'committees' is a decoy

examples.text: Everyone on the committees have signed the form.
examples.label: 'Everyone' wrongly treated as plural

examples.text: Neither the assistant nor the visiting researchers have the final report.
examples.label: The nearer subject researchers is plural, so have agrees.

sections.tip: When each, everyone, every one, either, or neither is the subject, use singular agreement. In either/or and neither/nor pairs, use the nearer subject instead.

sections.heading: Keep tense consistent
body: Match tense to the event’s time and its relationship to other events. Use surrounding verbs and time clues; a justified change in time can require a tense change.
Past perfect, “had finished,” places an action before another past action. Do not change tense merely because an answer sounds smoother.

examples.text: She studied all night and then aced the exam.
examples.label: Both verbs stay in the past

examples.text: She studied all night and then aces the exam.
examples.label: Unjustified shift to present

sections.tip: Read the sentence before and after the underlined verb. Match their tense unless the text signals a real change in time.

sections.heading: Irregular verbs: past vs. past participle
body: After have, has, or had, use a special verb form called the past participle: had run, swum, drunk, begun, sung, rung, written, broken.
Compare the simple past: ran, swam, drank, began, sang, rang, wrote, broke. A form such as sung needs its helping verb to serve as the main verb.
Lay means place an object: lay, laid, have laid. Lie means recline: lie, lay, have lain. Check whether the verb takes an object before selecting its form.

examples.text: By Friday she had run twelve miles.
examples.label: Participle 'run' after 'had'

examples.text: By Friday she had ran twelve miles.
examples.label: Simple past 'ran' wrongly used after 'had'

examples.text: The patient lay down while the assistant laid a tray beside the bed.
examples.label: Lay is past-tense reclining; laid places the object tray.

sections.tip: After 'have/has/had,' use the participle: 'had run,' 'had swum,' 'had begun.' Never 'had ran,' 'had swam,' 'had began.'

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: When choices are forms of one verb, check subject agreement, time, and verb form.

Cross out phrases between subject and verb. Match one or more than one, check when the event happens, and use the past-participle form after have/has/had. A choice can pass one check and fail another.
sections.tip: If two choices commit the same error, such as two plural verbs for a singular subject, eliminate both at once. The right answer must stand apart from every other choice.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: inverted subjects and changes in time
body: A subject can come after its verb: Inside the case lies a manuscript. Locate the head noun, not the nearby plural inside a phrase or relative clause.

A shift in tense is justified when time changes. A historical account can use past tense for a discovery and present tense for a fact still true. Keep the sentence's claim, its time signals, and agreement together.

examples.text: Among the drawings recovered from the attic lies a map that still shows the old boundary.
examples.label: Map controls lies despite drawings; still shows expresses the map’s continuing content.

examples.text: Among the drawings recovered from the attic lie a map that still shows the old boundary.
examples.label: The plural verb is attracted to drawings instead of agreeing with map.

examples.text: In 1986, the survey team recorded the river’s course. The river still follows that course today.
examples.label: Recorded belongs to the historical survey; follows states the river’s continuing present course.

sections.tip: Find the head subject first; determine the time of the specific claim second.

check.stem: The collection of vintage cars [[are]] displayed in the old warehouse.
check.explanation: The subject is 'collection,' which is singular, so 'is' agrees. 'Are,' 'were,' and 'have been' are all plural forms that wrongly agree with 'cars,' a noun trapped inside the prepositional phrase 'of vintage cars.'

check.stem: Each of the contestants [[have]] practiced for months.
check.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes 'has.' 'Have' wrongly treats the plural 'contestants' as the subject, but that noun sits inside the prepositional phrase 'of the contestants.' 'Are' and 'were' are plural, and they turn the sentence into a passive ('are practiced') that makes no sense with 'for months.'

check.stem: Last summer we hiked every morning and [[swim]] in the lake each afternoon.
check.explanation: The time clue 'last summer' and the parallel past-tense verb 'hiked' require the simple past 'swam.' 'Swim' is present tense, 'swum' is a participle that cannot stand without a helping verb, and 'had swum' wrongly shifts to the past perfect for an action that happened at the same time as the hiking.
